solutions.check: bars rebuilt from the blog's numbered answers (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Begin from comedy movie's end — natural order's reversed

parts.note: com is the short form of comedy, as in sitcom and romcom

indicators.note: an end is the final point of a word, so only its closing letter is kept

parts.note: the final letter of movie

indicators.note: turned back to front, so the pair of letters is read from right to left

parts.note: N is an abbreviation for natural
O is an abbreviation for order, as in OBE

explanation.surface: Advice to start watching a comedy film from its ending, turning the usual order of things upside down.
explanation.walkthrough: 'From' is only a link here. The two abbreviations N and O are read backwards to make ON, after COM and E.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrasal verb can mean to start or set in, as when rain or night comes on gradually.

clue.text: Taxis carrying popular hampers

indicators.note: to carry something is to hold it inside, so one piece sits within the other

parts.note: cabs are taxis
in means fashionable or popular

explanation.surface: Cabs ferrying a well-loved picnic basket, or taxis full of fashionable hampers.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hampers' looks like a noun for baskets, but it is a verb: to cabin is an old word meaning to confine or cramp.
explanation.definitionFit: Cabin as a verb means to shut up in a small space, restricting movement just as hampering does.

clue.text: Spoiled stroke spoiled music with eccentricity

indicators.note: something spoiled is damaged and messed about, so its letters are jumbled

parts.note: taken as written
e is the mathematical symbol for the eccentricity of a conic

explanation.surface: A botched shot, and a ruined piece of music played with some oddity.
explanation.walkthrough: The repeated 'spoiled' does two jobs: the first belongs to the definition, the second shuffles the letters.
explanation.definitionFit: In snooker or billiards a miscue is a shot where the cue tip slips off the ball, a botched stroke.

clue.text: Shamefully retract fresh reasons to wed

indicators.note: fresh means new, so the letters are made into a new arrangement

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone humiliatingly backing out after finding new reasons to marry.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole twelve-letter fodder sits in plain view after 'fresh'.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom means to admit humbly that something you said was wrong, taking back a statement with embarrassment.

clue.text: Honk if standing for English in forgotten bit of church

indicators.note: to stand for something is to take its place, so one letter is swapped for another

parts.note: taken as written
E is the abbreviation for English
nef is an obsolete word for the nave of a church

explanation.surface: A car horn sounding, if somewhere English in a church has been forgotten.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Forgotten' marks an obsolete word. In NEF the E is replaced by IF. Honk and niff are both British slang for a bad smell.
explanation.definitionFit: Both are informal British words for an unpleasant smell or stink.

clue.text: Small change for American perfumes

parts.note: S is the abbreviation for small
cents are the coins of US small change

explanation.surface: Swapping a few coins for American fragrances.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Change' suggests altering something, but here it is loose coins, and 'for American' says which currency.
explanation.definitionFit: Scents and perfumes are both fragrant liquids worn on the skin, so the words are synonyms.

clue.text: Is something hard to accomplish most dangerous?

parts.note: is shortens to 's, as in it's
Everest stands for any huge challenge

explanation.surface: A question whether the hardest challenge is also the riskiest.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Is' reads as the start of a question, but it is the contracted 's. Everest is used figuratively for any formidable task.
explanation.definitionFit: Severe can describe a grave or perilous condition, so the superlative fits the most perilous case.

clue.text: Vet direct from awful vermin case

parts.note: ex means direct from, as in goods sold ex works

indicators.note: awful means terrible or a mess, so the letters are thrown into disorder

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A vet getting orders straight from a dreadful case of pest infestation.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Vet' suggests an animal doctor and 'direct' an order, but vet is short for veteran and 'direct from' gives EX.
explanation.definitionFit: Vet is a common American shortening of veteran, a former member of the armed forces.

clue.text: Relative's bread not available

parts.note: naan or nan is an Indian flatbread
n/a is the abbreviation for not available

explanation.surface: A relation's loaf has run out.
explanation.walkthrough: The apostrophe s reads as possession but stands for 'is', joining definition and wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: Nanna is an affectionate family word for a grandmother, a close family member.

clue.text: Symbol of the Apostles, say, erected happily outside hospital

indicators.note: to sit outside something is to surround it, so one piece goes around another
done happily means freely and casually, so the letters fall into a loose new order

parts.note: taken as written
H is the abbreviation for hospital

explanation.surface: A religious emblem cheerfully put up outside a hospital.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Symbol' is the old church term for a creed (Latin symbolum), so the Apostles' Creed is the Symbol of the Apostles; 'say' marks it as an example.
explanation.definitionFit: A creed is a formal statement of belief; the traditional church name for such a statement is a symbol.

clue.text: Second English isle out for plant

parts.note: S is the abbreviation for second

indicators.note: out can mean out of order or wrong, so the letters are rearranged

parts.note: E is the abbreviation for English
taken as written

explanation.surface: A second English island is ruled out as a site for a plant.
explanation.walkthrough: Only the last word of the clue is the definition; everything before 'for' builds the letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Seseli is a genus of umbelliferous herbs related to parsley and carrot, so a plant name.

clue.text: Paradise Regained sadly cut dire greed and places for hives

indicators.note: sadly means in a sorry state, so the remaining letters are disordered
to cut is to take away, so some letters are removed from the long phrase

parts.note: the title of Milton's epic, taken as written
greed taken as written; dire tells you its letters need not be in order
taken as written

explanation.surface: A sorrowful note that Milton's Paradise Regained trimmed out terrible avarice, with a nod to beehives.
explanation.walkthrough: Remove the letters of GREED and AND from PARADISE REGAINED and rearrange the eight left over. Hives here are beehives, not the skin rash.
explanation.definitionFit: An apiary is a place where bees are kept, usually holding a number of beehives.

clue.text: Where to see blash run first?

parts.note: R is the cricket abbreviation for run
one means first, as in number one

explanation.surface: A question about where you would spot a sudden downpour running off first.
explanation.walkthrough: Both words are Scots: blash is a heavy splash of rain and a rone is a roof gutter or rainpipe, which is where rain runs.
explanation.definitionFit: Rainwater from a downpour flows along the roof gutter, so the Scots gutter is where such rain is seen.

clue.text: First for Biggles — air staff near ace

indicators.note: first means the opening position, so each named word supplies only its initial letter

parts.note: the initials of Biggles, air and staff
to can mean near or close by, as in close to

explanation.surface: Biggles the fictional flying ace, among air-force staff.
explanation.walkthrough: Biggles makes 'ace' look like a pilot, but it is a playing card: basto is the ace of clubs in old card games such as ombre and quadrille.
explanation.definitionFit: In ombre and quadrille the basto is the ace of clubs, always the third-highest trump.

clue.text: Rumpole's venues in fights about voided offence

indicators.note: about means around, so one piece wraps the other

parts.note: vies means competes or fights

indicators.note: voided means emptied, so the inside of the word is removed and only its outer letters stay

parts.note: sin is an offence; its outer letters are kept

explanation.surface: Where Rumpole of the Bailey works, amid fights over a dropped charge.
explanation.walkthrough: Rumpole, the barrister of the TV series, signals a legal term: a visne is a venue in law, the district a jury comes from.
explanation.definitionFit: Visne is an old legal word for venue, the neighbourhood from which a jury is drawn.

clue.text: Busy reasoning engaging modern passman?

indicators.note: to engage is to take in or hold, so one piece is held inside another

parts.note: inference is reasoning from evidence
a passman is a trusted prisoner; con is the modern word for a convict

explanation.surface: A busy logician working on a puzzle about a modern-day go-between.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Passman' looks like someone passing messages, but in prison slang it is an inmate trusted to move about, so a con.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone said to be in a meeting with colleagues is busy and cannot be disturbed, so the phrase means occupied.

clue.text: Good taste, for example, in English pike

parts.note: E is the abbreviation for English

indicators.note: to be in something is to sit inside it, so one piece is placed within another

parts.note: a pike and a lance are both long spears
eg is the abbreviation for for example

explanation.surface: Refined taste shown, say, by an English fish.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pike' suggests the fish, but it is the long spear here.
explanation.definitionFit: Elegance is refined grace and style, which is what good taste produces in dress or manner.

clue.text: Rarely passed through a verse, obsolete, about to rise

parts.note: a means per, as in ten pounds a day

indicators.note: something about to rise is going up, so one letter climbs higher in this down entry and the order changes

parts.note: V is the abbreviation for verse
something obsolete is dead

explanation.surface: A line of verse, long out of use, that has seldom been read through and is about to be revived.
explanation.walkthrough: In DEAD the letter A, standing for about, rises to the top of the word. 'Rarely' belongs to the definition: the sense of passing through is marked rare.
explanation.definitionFit: To pervade is to spread through; its older rare sense is simply to go or pass right through something.

clue.text: A pretty much uncommon tree

indicators.note: pretty much means nearly all, so the word loses its last letter

parts.note: taken as written
rare means uncommon

explanation.surface: A tree that is quite unusual.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pretty' looks like an adjective about the tree, but with 'much' it means almost.
explanation.definitionFit: The arar is a North African tree, the sandarac tree, whose resin is used in varnish.

clue.text: Obsequious Irishman's brass in bearing nut

parts.note: a brass sleeve is the lining inside a plain bearing
in printing an en is also called a nut

explanation.surface: An Irish sycophant with brass neck, carrying a nut for a bearing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Brass' suggests cheek or money, but in engineering a brass is the bush or sleeve lining a bearing. Printers call an en space a nut.
explanation.definitionFit: Sleeveen is an Irish word for a smooth-tongued, sly fawning person, so a flattering Irishman fits.

clue.text: Swamp's unusually vile

indicators.note: unusually means not in the normal way, so the letters take an abnormal order

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A complaint that a marsh is especially nasty.
explanation.walkthrough: The 's is 'is', linking the definition to the wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: Vlei is a South African word for low marshy ground where water collects, a seasonal swamp.

clue.text: Hair things for Sloane Rangers?

definitions.meaning: first meaning: styling products put on hair
second meaning: girls, as said in a posh upper-class accent

explanation.walkthrough: Sloane Rangers are fashionable upper-class young Londoners; in their drawl 'girls' comes out as a four-letter word, the things in the second reading.
explanation.definitionFit: Styling products for hair share the spelling with the plummy pronunciation of young women used by posh speakers.

clue.text: Natter with one about Scott's little curiosity

parts.note: to gab is to chatter or natter
I is the Roman numeral one
on means about, as in a talk on a topic

explanation.surface: Chatting with someone about a small oddity of Walter Scott's.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Scott's' marks a word used by Sir Walter Scott, who used it for a small curio or knick-knack.
explanation.definitionFit: Sir Walter Scott used gabion to mean a small curio or knick-knack collected by antiquarians.

clue.text: Old Russian units swarm in charges lacking commander's lead

indicators.note: in places one piece inside another
lacking means without, so a letter is taken away

parts.note: cares are charges, things in your keeping
the first letter of commander, the one taken away
to swarm up a rope or tree is to shin up it

explanation.surface: Old Russian army units charging in a mass, but without their commander at the front.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Units' suggests soldiers, as do 'swarm', 'charges' and 'commander', but these are units of length, and swarm means climb.
explanation.definitionFit: The arshin was an old Russian measure of length, about 71 centimetres.

clue.text: Hack mostly uninspired script

indicators.note: mostly means not quite all, so the final letter is dropped

parts.note: a nag or hack is a worn-out horse
arid means dull or uninspired

explanation.surface: A hack writer producing a largely dull script.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hack' and 'script' suggest a jobbing writer, but the hack is a horse.
explanation.definitionFit: Nagari is the writing system also called Devanagari, used for Sanskrit and Hindi.

clue.text: Watergate, as it was director spoke brazenly for Americans

parts.note: sasse is an obsolete word for a sluice or canal lock, a water gate
D is the abbreviation for director

explanation.surface: The Watergate scandal, as it unfolded, with a director making bold statements for an American audience.
explanation.walkthrough: Watergate looks like the Nixon scandal, but read as a water gate it is a sluice; 'as it was' marks an obsolete word.
explanation.definitionFit: Sass is American slang for cheek, so to sass someone is to answer back impudently.

clue.text: Women in interval look informally

indicators.note: in places one piece inside another

parts.note: a gap is an interval
W is the abbreviation for women

explanation.surface: Women at the theatre interval glancing around casually.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Informally' is part of the definition, marking a slang word.
explanation.definitionFit: To gawp is British slang for staring openly and stupidly at something.

clue.text: Piercing air-conditioning on sandgroper's truck?

parts.note: AC is the abbreviation for air-conditioning
a sandgroper is a Western Australian, and ute is Australian for a pick-up truck

explanation.surface: Whether air-conditioning in an Australian's pick-up could be ear-splitting.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down clue one piece written on another sits above it. Sandgroper is Australian slang for a Western Australian.
explanation.definitionFit: Acute and piercing both describe something sharp and intense, such as a pain or a sound.

clue.text: A restraint for gaoler

parts.note: taken as written
a dam holds back water, a restraint

explanation.surface: A device to hold back a prisoner, kept by a jailer.
explanation.walkthrough: Adam as a word for jailer is archaic, from Shakespeare's Comedy of Errors, where a sergeant is likened to Adam dressed in calf-skin.
explanation.definitionFit: In old usage Adam was a nickname for a sergeant or jailer, after a joke in Shakespeare's Comedy of Errors.

clue.text: Such as may be the stuff of a classic English flower

definitions.text: Such as may be the stuff of a classic English
definitions.meaning: first meaning: the core of a traditional English breakfast
second meaning: a popular name for bird's-foot trefoil, a yellow wild flower

explanation.walkthrough: 'English' is followed by an unstated noun, breakfast; the reader expects 'English flower' to be a phrase, like an English rose.
explanation.definitionFit: The fried pair is the heart of a full English breakfast, and the phrase is also a folk name for bird's-foot trefoil.

clue.text: One apparently restricts ebb and flow?

indicators.note: to restrict is to confine within limits, so the letters are held inside the words

parts.note: the letters run across the join of the two words

explanation.surface: A thing that seemingly limits the rise and fall of the tide.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface reads as a cryptic definition of a tide, but the letters are simply concealed in the first two words.
explanation.definitionFit: A neap tide is a tide of minimal range, so it is one particular instance of the sea's rise and fall.

clue.text: Hardened judge leaving hurt

indicators.note: leaving means departing, so a letter goes out of the word

parts.note: injured means hurt
J is the abbreviation for judge

explanation.surface: A tough judge walking away from an injury.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Leaving' could be a participle about the judge, but it removes a letter from the word for hurt.
explanation.definitionFit: Inured means accustomed to hardship and so toughened against it, the same sense as hardened.

clue.text: Gather lots before noon, when special

parts.note: am means ante meridiem, before midday
as means when, as in as I left
S is the abbreviation for special

explanation.surface: Collecting a great deal in the morning, when it is a special occasion.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Lots' seems the object of 'gather' and forms part of the definition, not the wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: To amass is to accumulate a large quantity, so it means collecting a great deal.

clue.text: Join squabble with no united edge

parts.note: a seam is a join

indicators.note: with no means lacking, so a letter is taken away

parts.note: to argue is to squabble
U is the abbreviation for united

explanation.surface: A divided group urged to join a quarrel with no united front.
explanation.walkthrough: Marge is a poetic word for margin, so the answer is the margin of the sea.
explanation.definitionFit: The seashore is the boundary of the sea, its border or margin, so it fits the definition.

clue.text: Born truly Asian from the east but one suddenly expelled irritant

parts.note: née marks a woman's maiden name, meaning born

indicators.note: in an across clue coming from the east means reading from right to left
but means except, so one letter for the number one is removed

parts.note: desi means authentically South Asian
I is the Roman numeral one

explanation.surface: Someone of genuine Asian birth sneezing out an irritant.
explanation.walkthrough: Neese is an old and dialect spelling of sneeze.
explanation.definitionFit: Sneezing is the sudden explosive expulsion of an irritant from the nose.

clue.text: Rendered with help mixed up Old Norse within

indicators.note: within places a piece inside another

parts.note: pied means jumbled, as printers' type is when it is pied
ON is the abbreviation for Old Norse

explanation.surface: A translation of Old Norse done with some help, but muddled.
explanation.walkthrough: A pony is American student slang for a crib or literal translation; to pony a text is to translate it with one.
explanation.definitionFit: To pony is to translate using a crib, so a text rendered with such aid has been ponied.
